name: Hair dough baking (wig curling)

card.summary: A historical wigmaking technique in which hair was enclosed in dough and baked in a baker's oven, used in the 17th-18th century wig trade to set and treat hair for fashionable wigs.
card.aka: Baking hair in dough, wig baking
card.note: A historical trade practice; documented mainly in the context of 18th-century French wigmaking.

quick.overview:
Hair dough baking was a trade method of the wigmaking era in which hair for wigs was packed in dough and baked in an oven, with local bakers doing the baking. It belongs to the world of 17th-18th century wigs, when full-bottomed and powdered wigs were standard dress for men of status.

The appearance payoff was the wig itself: well-prepared curls and moisture-retaining hair that held a fashionable shape. It is a historical practice, not a current styling method, and the best-documented detail is its taxation debate in France.
quick.how: Wig histories describe wigmakers having hair baked in dough at bakeries, with gingerbread bakers in Paris routinely supplying the dough, and the hair afterwards being made into wigs that were then powdered.
quick.risks: Little is documented about worker or customer harm. Historically, the practice surfaced in disputes over taxes and the freedom of commerce.

lead: Hair dough baking, sometimes described as a way of setting wig curls in a baker's oven, was part of how wigs were produced in 18th-century France.[1] Wigmakers had hair baked in dough, which Wikipedia's account says helped it retain moisture; in Paris, gingerbread bakers routinely baked the dough for them, while elsewhere in France it was not necessarily gingerbread.[1]

The technique served the larger goal of wigs as appearance: Louis XIII began wearing a wig in 1624 as he lost his hair, periwigs reached England with Charles II in 1660, and wig fashion spread across Europe under Louis XIV.[1] Finished wigs were powdered, first with scented low-grade flour and later with finely ground starch scented with orange flower, lavender or orris root.[1]

In 1705 a tax on hair-dough baking was proposed, and wigmakers in Grenoble protested that it would 'destroy the liberty of commerce'.[1] Wigs largely fell from fashion by the 1760s apart from some occupations, and the 1795 Duty on Hair Powder Act largely ended the fashion for wigs and powder.[1]

chain: Wig hair holds moisture and shape
angle.text: The method was part of producing the wig's curled, controlled look. It matters today as history: it shows how earlier eras made hair appear fuller and more ordered.

infobox: Local bakers, including Paris gingerbread bakers

paras: Early wigs were made by weaving root ends of hair onto three silk threads to form a fringe that was sewn to a net or foundation; in the 19th century wigmakers began knotting strands directly into foundations with a ventilating needle.[1] Hair was sorted so growth direction was maintained, and cheaper wigs used horse and goat hair.[1]
Baking hair in dough was one preparation step documented in French wigmaking.[1]
A tax on hair-dough baking was proposed in 1705, and Grenoble wigmakers protested.[1] A French wigmakers' guild was established in 1665.[1]

Periwigs reach England with the Restoration of Charles II.[1]
